$comment: Patches that play themselves. The defining property is that nobody is
holding a keyboard: the patch decides when the next event happens, and
usually what it is. This family is where 'it made a sound' is least
adequate as a check -- a krell that plays one note makes a sound.
Sources are techniques, not text: the method each idiom describes is
documented in the manuals and books named, and stated here in our words.

implies: different speeds coming from one clock
idioms.is: One clock divided several ways, each division triggering a different voice, so the parts drift in and out of phase without ever losing the pulse.
idioms.sounds_right_when: the parts line up periodically rather than randomly, and the whole thing stays in time.

topology.describe: a clock has to reach the divider
a division has to trigger something, or the divider is dividing into silence

common_mistakes.message: the divider has no clock to divide

axis.set_by: the clock modulator's own mode and ratio — a knob, not a cable, so every position on this axis patches identically
axis.$comment: One clock modulator between a clock and whatever it drives. Dividing, multiplying, swinging and spreading evenly are four settings of that one structure, so a checker reading cables cannot tell them apart. Separate records still earn their place: a person asking for swing is not asking for a divider.

implies: a pattern that slides between notes
idioms.is: A sample-and-hold clocked by an oscillator running below hearing, with the held voltage passed through a lag before it plays the note — so a repeating pattern arrives, and every interval in it is travelled rather than jumped.
idioms.sounds_right_when: a pattern recurs, and each move between its notes is audibly swooped rather than stepped.
idioms.source: ARP 2600 Patch Book to Behringer 2600 (Carl Bratcher), the Gliding Intervals patch

anchor.shows: a panel diagram captioned Gliding Intervals, with the third oscillator switched below hearing as the pattern source, the sample-and-hold in the signal path, the voltage processor's lag engaged, and notes to tune that oscillator for the pattern and the sample-and-hold's level for the size of the interval

topology.describe: something has to tell the sample-and-hold when to take a value — on the source instrument this is an oscillator switched below hearing, and its frequency is what sets the pattern
the held voltage has to pass through a lag, which is the whole difference between this and a stepped melody
the LAGGED voltage has to be what plays the note; patching the held voltage straight to pitch alongside it defeats the lag

listen_for.sounds_like: a line that never arrives cleanly: each note leans into the next, and because the sampled values repeat, the same swoops come round again. How far apart the notes are is one knob — the level of the sampled voltage — and how fast the pattern turns over is another.
listen_for.confusable_with: a stepped random melody, where every note lands square. If you cannot hear the journey between notes, nothing is lagging the voltage.

expect.why: fewer than three pitches is not a pattern, and the lag would have nothing to travel between

common_mistakes.message: nothing clocks the sample-and-hold, so it holds one value and the pattern never advances
the held voltage never reaches the lag, so the intervals step rather than glide
the lagged voltage never reaches a pitch input

idioms.is: A random voltage sampled to set an envelope's time, with the envelope's end-of-cycle retriggering it — so the patch plays itself and each note chooses how long the next one waits.
idioms.sounds_right_when: notes arrive at uneven, unpredictable intervals and never settle into a loop; the gaps vary as much as the notes.
idioms.source: Todd Barton's Krell patch, after the Barrons' Forbidden Planet score

topology.describe: a random voltage has to reach the envelope's time input — without it every note is the same length, which is a sequence, not a krell
the envelope's end-of-cycle has to retrigger it — without that loop nothing starts the next note and the patch plays once
the envelope has to open an amplifier, or the notes it is shaping are never heard

common_mistakes.message: the envelope never retriggers itself, so the patch plays a single note
nothing randomises the envelope's time, so every note is identical
there is no random source at all

idioms.is: Two oscillators cross-modulating through a shift register, so the register's output steers the oscillators that are clocking it — stepped chaos that never repeats but is never random either.
idioms.sounds_right_when: the pattern is clearly patterned and clearly unpredictable at the same time; small knob moves change its character completely.
idioms.source: Rob Hordijk's Rungler and Benjolin designs

topology.describe: an oscillator has to clock the register — that is what makes the chaos audio-rate rather than a slow random walk
the register has to modulate an oscillator back, or there is no feedback and no chaos

common_mistakes.message: the register never feeds back, so this is a modulated oscillator, not a rungler
nothing clocks the register from the audio path

idioms.is: Noise sampled on a clock to produce a new pitch each step — the simplest way a rack invents a melody.
idioms.sounds_right_when: each clock brings a new, unrelated pitch, held steady until the next one.
idioms.source: Allen Strange's account of sample-and-hold as a source of stepped voltage

listen_for.sounds_like: a new, unrelated note on every tick, each held dead steady until the next — no glide, no pattern, and no note more likely than any other
listen_for.confusable_with: a sampled periodic source, which comes back around; if you can hear the phrase repeat, the sample-and-hold is not being fed noise

expect.why: fewer than three pitches from a random source across a whole run means the sample-and-hold is barely being clocked

topology.describe: noise has to feed the sample-and-hold, or it samples something predictable
a clock has to tell it when to sample, or it never takes a new value
the held voltage has to reach a pitch input

common_mistakes.message: nothing clocks the sample-and-hold, so the pitch never changes
the sample-and-hold has nothing to sample

idioms.is: A clocked shift register fed by noise, whose loop can be locked or allowed to mutate — a melody that repeats until you let it change.
idioms.sounds_right_when: a phrase repeats recognisably, then alters by one note rather than becoming a new phrase.
idioms.source: Music Thing Modular's Turing Machine; the technique is a clocked shift register

topology.describe: the register has to be clocked, or the sequence never advances
the register's voltage has to reach a pitch input, or there is no melody to hear

common_mistakes.message: nothing clocks the register, so it holds one value forever
the sequence never reaches a pitch input, so nothing plays it

idioms.is: A sustained voice with at least two modulators running at different, unrelated rates, so the timbre keeps moving and the patch never lands in the same place twice.
idioms.sounds_right_when: it holds without stopping, and what you hear a minute in is audibly different from the start — not louder or quieter, but different in colour.
idioms.source: Bjørn & Meyer's treatment of unsynchronised modulation in ambient patches

topology.describe: the oscillator has to reach a filter, or there is nothing for the modulation to shape
a modulator has to move the filter, or this is a tone rather than a drone that evolves
a second, unrelated modulator has to move something else — with only one, the patch repeats on that modulator's cycle

common_mistakes.message: nothing modulates the filter, so this is a tone, not an evolving drone
only one modulator, so the patch repeats exactly on its cycle
the oscillator never reaches the filter
